newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish finance minister wants budget ready by Oct.
newsitem.headline: Polish finance minister wants budget ready by Oct.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday he wanted the government to submit the 1998 budget draft to parliament after the September 21 parliamentary polls but before the end of the month.
"We want the budget to be ready by the end of September so as the prime minister can submit his resignation and the budget," Belka told a news briefing.

He said he was confident the cabinet would approve the budget's macroeconomic assumptions, total revenues and spending levels at its session on Thursday so as the ministry could start working on spending levels for particular ministries. @
The proposals were criticised on Wednesday by the junior group in the government coalition, the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), which said the draft's aim to cool domestic demand could hurt growth.
Belka confirmed the finance ministry had proposed the 1998 budget deficit at 1.9 percent of gross domestic product, compared with 2.8 percent planned for 1997.
The daily Rzeczpospolita said earlier in the day the deficit would amount to 9.6 billion zlotys, with revenues at 133.3 billion zlotys and spending at 142.9 billion zlotys. @
Belka said he wanted to wait until Thursday with commenting on the report.
He said the lower budget deficit was meant to stifle internal demand, whose recent growth had dangerously boosted current account deficit.

Belka reiterated his earlier forecast that the current account deficit would reach $6 billion at the end of the year from $1.35 billion in 1996, and trade deficit about $12 billion from $8.2 billion last year.
He said these deficit levels were not dangerous for the economy. @
He also said the budget draft assummed the zloty would be devalued by 7-10 percent next year.
Belka confirmed the budget assummed that year-on-year inflation would fall in December next year 9.5 percent from 14.6 percent in May and less than 13 percent planned for December 1997.
